title: Gaps in the rationals
objectives: Show that the rationals have gaps, such as a missing square root of 2.

screens.title: Hunting for a square root of 2
screens.prose: We want a fraction $\tfrac pq$ whose square is exactly 2. The dots mark two simple guesses on the curve $y = x^2$. Three better guesses are already worked out in the table.

state.caption: The curve $y = x^2$ meets the line $y = 2$ at the number we want.

screens.question: Fill in the squares of $\tfrac32$ and $\tfrac75$ as decimals.

hints.text: Square the top and the bottom: $\left(\tfrac pq\right)^2 = \tfrac{p^2}{q^2}$.

feedback.correct: 2.25 overshoots and 1.96 falls short. The other three come closer, but none hits 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square the top and the bottom of each fraction, then divide.

explain.text: $\tfrac94 = 2.25$ sits above the line and $\tfrac{49}{25} = 1.96$ below it. The table's fractions land closer each time. Every square misses 2, above or below.

screens.title: Measure the miss
screens.prose: How badly does each fraction miss? If $\tfrac{p^2}{q^2} = 2$, then $p^2 - 2q^2 = 0$. So we work out $p^2 - 2q^2$ for each fraction, in whole numbers.

state.caption: The last three fractions sit almost on the crossing point.

screens.question: Fill in $p^2 - 2q^2$ for each row.

hints.text: Square $p$, square $q$, double the second, subtract.
First row: $9 - 2 \times 4 = 1$. Second row: $49 - 2 \times 25$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $p^2$ and $2q^2$ separately, then subtract. Keep any minus sign.

byKey.r1c2: For $\tfrac75$: $49 - 2 \times 25 = 49 - 50 = -1$. The square falls short, so the sign is negative.

explain.text: The values run $1, -1, 1, -1, 1$, never 0. Dividing by $q^2$, each square misses 2 by exactly $\tfrac{1}{q^2}$. The miss shrinks as $q$ grows, but it never vanishes.

screens.title: Zoom in on the crossing point
screens.prose: Every stop of this point is a decimal with four places, so a fraction. Drag it near the three fractions and watch $x^2$ in the caption.
screens.question: Can you make $x^2$ read exactly 2?

options.text: No. At 1.4142 it is just below 2; at 1.4143 it is just above.

options.why: You read 1.4142 as $\sqrt2$. Its square is $1.99996164$, a little short of 2.

options.text: Yes, if the point could stop at more decimal places.
options.why: You expected finer stops to hit 2. Each stop is still a fraction, and no fraction squares to 2, as we now prove.
You trusted a close fraction. The table showed $\tfrac{99}{70}$ squares to $2.000204$.

hints.text: Drag the point to 1.4142, then one stop to the right.
The square jumps from below 2 to above 2 between two stops, so no stop gives exactly 2.

feedback.correct: Right. The square jumps over 2 between neighbouring stops. A real number that is no fraction is called **irrational**.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag the point to 1.4142 and to 1.4143, and read the square each time.

explain.text: 1.4142 squares to $1.99996$ and 1.4143 to $2.00024$, so the square skips 2. Every stop is a fraction, and so is every finer stop. A number that is no fraction is **irrational**; we now prove $\sqrt2$ is one.

screens.title: The first line
screens.prose: We prove the claim: **no fraction squares to 2**, so $\sqrt2$ is irrational. As in the proof course's lesson on contradiction, we suppose the claim fails. Then we reason until something impossible follows.
screens.question: Which line should the proof start with?

options.text: Suppose $\sqrt2 = \tfrac pq$ for integers $p, q$ with $q \ne 0$, in lowest terms.

options.why: You supposed what we want to prove. A proof by contradiction supposes the opposite of the claim.
You picked one fraction. Ruling it out leaves infinitely many others, so the supposition must use letters.

options.text: Suppose $\sqrt2 = \tfrac pq$ for integers $p, q$ with $q \ne 0$.
options.why: You left out lowest terms. Later we find $p$ and $q$ both even, which clashes only with lowest terms.

hints.text: The claim is that something does not exist. What is its opposite?
The opposite of no fraction works is some fraction works.
Any fraction can be cancelled to lowest terms, so we may also assume that.

feedback.correct: Right. Some fraction, written with letters, cancelled to lowest terms.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Suppose the opposite of the claim, for a general fraction.

explain.text: The claim says no fraction works, so its opposite is that some fraction $\tfrac pq$ does. Every fraction cancels to lowest terms, so assuming that costs nothing. It is the line the contradiction will hit.

screens.title: Why is $p$ even?
screens.prose: Squaring $\sqrt2 = \tfrac pq$ gives $p^2 = 2q^2$, so $p^2$ is even. The next line reads: so $p$ is even. A reader will ask why.
screens.question: Which reason makes that line safe?

options.text: If $p$ were odd, $p = 2k + 1$, then $p^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1$ would be odd.

options.why: You said every square is even, but $3^2 = 9$ is odd.
You read $\sqrt2\, q$ as 2 times an integer. $\sqrt2$ is not 2, and we do not know it is a fraction.
You checked examples. The line must hold for every integer $p$.

hints.text: Prove the contrapositive: if $p$ is odd, then $p^2$ is odd.
Write an odd $p$ as $2k + 1$ and square it.

feedback.correct: Right. An odd number squared is odd, so an even square has an even root.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a reason that covers every integer $p$.

explain.text: $(2k + 1)^2 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1$ is odd. So if $p^2$ is even, $p$ cannot be odd. That is the contrapositive from the proof course.

screens.title: Substitute
screens.prose: Now $p$ is even, so we write $p = 2k$ for an integer $k$. Put this into $p^2 = 2q^2$.
screens.question: Then $q^2$ equals what, in terms of $k$?

hints.text: Square $2k$ first.
Divide both sides of $4k^2 = 2q^2$ by 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square $2k$, set it equal to $2q^2$, then solve for $q^2$.

byKey.nodiv: You stopped at $(2k)^2 = 4k^2$. That equals $2q^2$, so divide both sides by 2.
byKey.nosq: You wrote $p^2$ as $2k^2$. Square the 2 as well: $(2k)^2 = 4k^2$.

explain.text: $(2k)^2 = 4k^2 = 2q^2$, and dividing by 2 gives $q^2 = 2k^2$. So $q^2$ is even. By the same reason as before, $q$ is even.

screens.title: The whole proof
screens.prose: Here is the proof in seven lines, shuffled. Two extra lines are flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: Suppose $\sqrt2 = \tfrac pq$ for integers $p, q$ with $q \ne 0$, in lowest terms.
An odd number squared is odd, so $p$ is even: $p = 2k$ for an integer $k$.
By the same reason, $q$ is even.
So 2 divides both $p$ and $q$, against lowest terms.
So the supposition is false: $\sqrt2$ is irrational. $\blacksquare$

lines.why: You used the line that supposes the claim itself. We must suppose its opposite.

lines.text: Every square is even, so $p$ is even.
lines.why: You used the line that says every square is even. $3^2 = 9$ is odd.

hints.text: Start with the supposition, end with its downfall.
After $p = 2k$, substitute and look at $q$.
Order: suppose, square, $p$ even, $q^2 = 2k^2$, $q$ even, clash, conclude.

feedback.correct: Right. Seven lines, each from the one before.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line should follow from the lines above it.

byKey.d1: You used the line supposing $\sqrt2$ is irrational. That is the claim, so the proof would assume its own conclusion.
byKey.d2: You used the line saying every square is even. $3^2 = 9$ is odd; the reason is that odd squares are odd.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: We suppose a fraction in lowest terms, then show 2 divides $p$ and then $q$. That contradicts lowest terms. So no such fraction exists.

screens.title: Proof by contradiction
screens.prose:
To prove a claim $P$, suppose $\lnot P$ and reason until two lines clash. Here the supposition led to

$$\sqrt2 = \tfrac pq \text{ in lowest terms} \;\Rightarrow\; 2 \mid p \text{ and } 2 \mid q.$$
screens.question: Which two statements clash?

options.text: 2 divides $p$ and $q$, yet $\tfrac pq$ is in lowest terms.

options.why: You called $p^2 = 2q^2$ impossible. That is what we want to show, so it cannot be the clash.
You picked two lines that agree. Both follow from the supposition and sit happily together.

options.text: The decimals of $\sqrt2$ never repeat, yet $\tfrac pq$ repeats.
options.why: You used decimals. Nothing in the proof shows they never repeat; that is the claim in disguise.

hints.text: Which line was assumed, and which line was proved?
The supposition said lowest terms.
Lowest terms means $p$ and $q$ share no factor, but we showed both are even.

feedback.correct: Right. The proved line clashes with the supposed one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a proved line that contradicts the first line.

explain.text: Lowest terms means no common factor above 1. We proved 2 divides both. A statement and its opposite cannot both hold, so the supposition was false.

screens.title: Copying the proof for $\sqrt4$
screens.prose: A classmate copies the proof for $\sqrt4$, with 4 for 2. But $\sqrt4 = \tfrac21$, so some line must be broken.

rows: So $p$ and $q$ share the factor 4: a contradiction. $\blacksquare$

screens.question: Tap the first line that does not follow.

hints.text: Test each line on a small example.
Try line 3 with $p = 6$.
$6^2 = 36$ is divisible by 4, but 6 is not. Line 3 fails.

feedback.correct: Right. $6^2 = 36$ is a multiple of 4, but 6 is not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the first line that its predecessor does not support.

byKey.r1: Line 2 is fine: $p^2 = 4q^2$ is 4 times a whole number.
byKey.r3: Line 4 follows from line 3 by substitution. The fault is earlier.
byKey.r4: Line 5 repeats the move of line 3. That move first appears, and first fails, in line 3.
byKey.r5: Line 6 would follow if lines 3 and 5 held. The fault is in a move before it.
byKey.r0: Line 1 is a fair supposition: every fraction has lowest terms.

explain.text: For 2 the move works because 2 is prime: if 2 divides $p \cdot p$, it divides $p$. 4 is not prime, and $p = 6$ breaks the move. A proof of a false claim always has a broken line.

screens.title: The same proof for $\sqrt3$
screens.prose: The proof also shows $\sqrt3$ is irrational, with 3 for 2. Line 3 becomes: 3 divides $p^2$, so 3 divides $p$. The table checks the remainders for $p = 1$ to 6.

state.caption: $p^2$ is a multiple of 3 only in the rows where $p$ is.

screens.question: Why is that line safe for 3, when the same move failed for 4?

options.text: 3 is prime: if 3 divides $p \cdot p$, it divides a factor, $p$.

options.why: You leaned on 3 being odd. 9 is odd too, and 9 divides $6^2 = 36$ but not 6.
You said 3 divides every square. $2^2 = 4$ leaves remainder 1.
You checked examples. The line must hold for every $p$; that needs a reason.

hints.text: What does 3 have that 4 lacks?
4 = 2 × 2 splits; 3 does not.
A prime dividing a product divides one of its factors. Here both factors are $p$.

feedback.correct: Right. Primes pass from a product to a factor.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find a reason that works for every $p$ and fails for 4.

explain.text: If a prime divides $p \cdot p$, it divides $p$. 3 is prime; 4 and 9 are not. So the proof works for $\sqrt3$ and $\sqrt5$, but not word for word for $\sqrt4$.

screens.title: Floats are fractions
screens.prose: A float is a fraction whose denominator is a power of 2. So `2 ** 0.5` is a fraction near $\sqrt2$, and its square misses 2. A pricing library checks that two model prices, `a` and `b`, agree.
screens.question: Which test should it use?

options.why: You compared floats exactly. `(2 ** 0.5) ** 2 == 2` is already `False`.
You rounded to whole pounds. Then £9.60 and £10.40 would agree.
You compared the printed digits. That is still exact equality, one character at a time.

hints.text: The square of a float near $\sqrt2$ is a float near 2.
Exact tests fail on tiny errors like 0.0000000000000004.
Accept a difference below a small tolerance.

feedback.correct: Right. Compare within a tolerance, never exactly.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choose a test that forgives an error in the 16th digit but not a real difference.

explain.text: No fraction squares to 2, so no float does either. The stored square misses by about $4 \times 10^{-16}$. A tolerance such as $10^{-9}$ absorbs that and still catches real gaps.

ideas: No fraction squares to 2: for $\tfrac pq$ near $\sqrt2$, $p^2 - 2q^2$ is never 0.
Suppose $\sqrt2 = \tfrac pq$ in lowest terms. Then 2 divides $p$ and $q$, a contradiction.
The move from $n \mid p^2$ to $n \mid p$ works for a prime $n$, so $\sqrt3$ and $\sqrt5$ are irrational too.

formula.name: $\sqrt2$ is irrational
formula.tex: \sqrt2 = \tfrac pq \text{ in lowest terms} \;\Rightarrow\; 2 \mid p \text{ and } 2 \mid q
formula.note: The clash with lowest terms shows $\sqrt2 \notin \mathbb{Q}$.

summary.trap: “4 divides $p^2$, so 4 divides $p$” is false: $6^2 = 36$. The move needs a prime.

quiz.prose: $\tfrac{577}{408}$ is an even closer fraction to $\sqrt2$.
quiz.question: Work out $577^2 - 2 \times 408^2$.

byKey.zero: You expected 0. That would make $\tfrac{577}{408}$ exactly $\sqrt2$, which the proof rules out.
byKey.neg: Check the sign: $577^2 = 332929$ is bigger than $2 \times 408^2 = 332928$.

explain.text: $577^2 = 332929$ and $408^2 = 166464$, so $2 \times 408^2 = 332928$. The difference is 1, never 0, as the proof says.

quiz.prose: A classmate copies the proof for $\sqrt{9/4}$: suppose $\sqrt{9/4} = \tfrac pq$ in lowest terms.
quiz.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: $\sqrt{9/4} = \tfrac32$ is rational, so the copied proof must break somewhere.
The copied proof shows $\sqrt{9/4}$ is irrational.
options.why: You trusted the copy. $\left(\tfrac32\right)^2 = \tfrac94$, so the root is a fraction.

options.text: Only roots of whole numbers can be rational.
options.why: You ruled out roots of fractions. $\tfrac94$ is not whole, yet its root $\tfrac32$ is rational.

options.text: The proof for $\sqrt2$ works for any number under the root.
options.why: You stretched the proof too far. It relies on 2 being prime; for $\tfrac94$ no clash arises.

explain.text: $\left(\tfrac32\right)^2 = \tfrac94$, so $\sqrt{9/4}$ is rational. Any copy of the proof for it must contain a false line. Checking a claim on a known case is a fast way to catch a broken proof.

quiz.prose: Use the proof and its copies.
quiz.question: Which of these numbers are irrational? Select all that apply.

options.why: You called $\sqrt{16}$ irrational. It equals 4.
You picked a fraction close to $\sqrt2$. It is still a fraction, so rational.
You picked $\sqrt{9/4}$. It equals $\tfrac32$.

feedback.correct: Right. $\sqrt3$ and $\sqrt5$: the proof works because 3 and 5 are prime.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Simplify each number first, then ask whether the proof applies.

explain.text: 3 and 5 are prime, so the proof goes through for their roots. $\sqrt{16} = 4$ and $\sqrt{9/4} = \tfrac32$ are rational. $\tfrac{99}{70}$ is a fraction by definition.

options.text: 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 are stored as nearby fractions with power-of-two denominators.

options.why: You blamed the adding. The sum is computed exactly; the inputs were already rounded.
You called 0.1 irrational. It is $\tfrac{1}{10}$, just not a fraction with a power-of-two denominator.

options.text: Floats must be added in a fixed order.
options.why: You blamed the order. Swapping to `0.2 + 0.1` gives the same `False`.

feedback.correct: Right. A tenth has no exact float.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which fractions a float can hold exactly.

explain.text: A float holds fractions $\tfrac{m}{2^k}$ only. $\tfrac{1}{10}$ is not one, so it is stored as the nearest one. The rounding errors add to `0.30000000000000004`.
